Prompt Engineering vs Context Engineering

Craft clear instructions and assemble the information they need. Explore how prompts, retrieval, memory, tools, and history work together across an AI workflow.

Explore the slides

Two complementary engineering disciplines

Prompt engineering specifies what the model should do and how it should respond. Context engineering decides which information the model receives on each turn, how much fits the budget, and what should persist for later. The prompt is one layer within that larger information environment.

Prompt engineering and context engineering compared
DimensionPrompt engineeringContext engineering
FocusInstructions, examples, and output formatInformation selection and assembly
InputsRole, task, constraints, and demonstrationsDocuments, memories, tools, history, and state
Time horizonA specific instruction or interactionInformation across turns and workflow steps
Typical failureAmbiguity or poor format adherenceMissing, irrelevant, stale, or conflicting evidence
EvaluationInstruction adherence and prompt comparisonsRetrieval, faithfulness, token budget, and task success

Write, select, compress, and isolate

  • Write: save plans, notes, or memories outside the active window.
  • Select: retrieve relevant documents, memories, and tool definitions for the current step.
  • Compress: summarize older turns and remove stale or unnecessary content.
  • Isolate: separate subtasks or state so each context remains focused.

How the layers work together

A request triggers selection of relevant knowledge, memory, and tools. The system trims that material to its budget and fills a prompt template with role, rules, context, and the query. After the model call, useful results can be saved as state or notes for the next turn.

Diagnose the right layer

First check whether the information needed to answer was present and relevant. If it was missing, improve retrieval and context assembly. Then examine whether the instructions clearly specify the task, constraints, and output. Keep separate measures for retrieval quality, grounded answers, instruction adherence, and multi-turn task completion.

Read slide text
Why the Shift to Context Engineering Agents, long contexts and the limits of clever wording “the delicate art and science of filling the context window” Andrej Karpathy, June 2025 “providing all the context for the task to be plausibly solvable” Tobi Lütke, Shopify CEO, June 2025 “the natural progression of prompt engineering” Anthropic Applied AI team, Sept 2025 1 Agents run in loops An agent calls tools turn after turn, so its context grows with every step and must be curated continuously, not written once. 2 Bigger windows ≠ better answers Chroma tested 18 LLMs in 2025: reliability fell as input length grew, even on simple tasks. 3 Prompts became software In production apps the prompt is a template filled with retrieved data, memory, tool results and history.

Slide 5: The Prompt Is One Layer of Context

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
The Prompt Is One Layer of the Context Everything the model sees on a single turn System instructions Role, rules, tone PROMPT Few-shot examples Demonstrations of good output PROMPT Tool definitions Names, descriptions, schemas CONTEXT Retrieved knowledge RAG chunks, search results CONTEXT Long-term memory User facts, past decisions CONTEXT History & tool results Recent turns, observations, state CONTEXT Current request The question and output spec PROMPT Prompt engineering asks How should the instruction be worded, structured and exemplified? Context engineering asks What belongs in the window at all — on this turn, within this token budget? Every layer competes for the same finite attention budget.

Slide 6: Anatomy of a Strong Prompt

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Anatomy of a Strong Prompt Six building blocks that remove ambiguity Role Who the model should be You are a senior contracts analyst. Task One specific, verifiable job Extract renewal and termination terms. Context Background the task depends on The client is a 40-person SaaS startup. Constraints Rules, boundaries, what to avoid Cite clause numbers. No legal advice. Output format The exact shape of the answer Table: term, clause, summary, risk. Examples Show, don't only tell One worked row of the table.

Slide 7: Core Prompting Techniques

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Core Prompting Techniques Use the lightest technique that gets reliable results TECHNIQUE WHAT IT DOES BEST FOR Zero-shot A clear instruction with no examples Simple, well-known tasks Few-shot Two to five input → output examples Format, tone, edge cases Chain-of-thought Ask the model to reason step by step before answering Math, logic, multi-step analysis Role prompting Assign a persona and level of expertise Domain voice and depth Structured prompts Delimit sections with XML tags; request JSON or a schema Long inputs, parsing, tool calls Prompt chaining Split a job into a sequence of smaller prompts Complex workflows, easier debugging

Slide 8: Prompt Engineering in Action

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Prompt Engineering in Action Same model, same document — a rewritten instruction BEFORE Summarize this contract. Typical result • Generic paragraph, different every run • Key dates and notice periods missed • No clause references to check • Length and format unpredictable <role>You are a contracts analyst for a SaaS startup.</role> <task>Extract renewal, termination and pricing terms from <contract>.</task> <rules> - Quote the clause number for every item. - If a term is missing, write "Not stated". - Do not give legal advice. </rules> <format>Markdown table: Term | Clause | Summary | Risk (Low/Med/High) </format> <contract>{contract_text}</contract> AFTER Still one moment in time: no memory, no retrieval, no tools. That is where context engineering takes over.

Slide 9: Four Context Engineering Strategies

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Four Context Engineering Strategies Write, select, compress and isolate (LangChain, July 2025) Write Save information outside the window so it survives across steps. • Scratchpads and plans • Long-term memory stores • Progress notes files Select Pull in only what the current step needs. • RAG over documents • Memory retrieval • Choosing tools from a large set Compress Keep only the tokens the task requires. • Summarize old turns • Trim message history • Clear stale tool results Isolate Split context across separate windows. • Sub-agents per subtask • Sandboxed tool execution • State fields hidden from the LLM Guiding principle: find “the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens” for the outcome you want — Anthropic, 2025

Slide 10: Designing Each Layer of Context

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Designing Each Layer of Context Practical guidance for agents that run over many turns System prompt: find the right altitude Too rigid Hard-coded if-else rules; brittle and costly to maintain Right altitude Specific enough to guide, flexible enough to generalize; clear sections Too vague High-level wishes that assume shared context Minimal, distinct tools If a human can't say which tool fits, the model can't either. Canonical examples A few diverse examples beat a long list of edge cases. Just-in-time retrieval Keep references such as file paths or IDs; load data when needed. Compaction and notes Summarize near the limit; keep a progress file outside the window. Sub-agents Deep work in clean windows; return condensed summaries of ~1–2k tokens. Source: Anthropic, “Effective context engineering for AI agents”, September 2025.

Slide 11: How Long Contexts Fail

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
How Long Contexts Fail More tokens is not more understanding Lost in the middle Recall is strongest at the start and end of a long input, weakest in the middle. Fix: Put critical facts at the edges; rerank retrieved chunks. Context rot Reliability falls as input length grows, even on simple tasks. Fix: Select and trim; keep each window focused. Context poisoning A hallucination enters the context and is referenced again and again. Fix: Validate before writing to memory; quarantine threads. Context distraction The context grows so long the model over-relies on it instead of its training. Fix: Summarize and compact long histories. Context confusion Irrelevant tools or documents in the window sway the answer. Fix: Select tools and documents per step. Context clash New information contradicts what is already in the context. Fix: Prune stale content; isolate subtasks. Sources: Liu et al., “Lost in the Middle” (TACL 2024); Chroma, “Context Rot” (2025, 18 models); Breunig, “How Long Contexts Fail” (2025).

Slide 12: Challenges: Prompt vs Context

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Challenges: Prompt vs Context Prompting is for a moment. Context is for conversation Brittleness of Prompt Fragility of Context Ambiguity: Vague instructions lead to inconsistent results. Maintenance: Manually managing thousands of prompts doesn't scale. Sensitivity: Minor word changes can break a perfectly good prompt. Lost in the Middle: AI struggles to recall info from the center of long contexts. Integration Failure: Garbage retrieved from the RAG pipeline leads to garbage output. Noise & Rot: Irrelevant or outdated information degrades performance. Symptom: An instruction fails to produce the desired output. Symptom: An instruction produces an inconsistent or hallucinatory output, often due to bad data Scalability & Maintenance: Manually creating and maintaining thousands of specific prompts is labor-intensive and doesn't scale. Retrieval & Integration Failures: A "Garbage In, Garbage Out" scenario where flawed data from the RAG pipeline leads to a flawed final answer. Core Problem: The instruction itself is ambiguous or easily misinterpreted by the AI. Environment: The information environment provided to the AI is flawed or incomplete.

Slide 13: How They Work Together

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
How They Work Together Context engineering builds the window; prompt engineering shapes the instruction Request User question or agent step Select Retrieve docs, memories, tools Compress Trim and summarize to budget Assemble Template: role, rules, context, query LLM call Generate answer or tool call Write back Update memory, notes, state next turn Context engineering owns What goes in, how much, from where, and what gets saved for later. Prompt engineering owns The template: role, rules, structure, output format and examples.

Slide 14: Assembling Context with LangChain

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
In Code: Assembling Context with LangChain One function, both disciplines prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([ ("system", "You are a support agent for {product}.\n" "Answer only from <docs>. If unsure, say so.\n" "<docs>{docs}</docs>\n<memory>{memory}</memory>"), MessagesPlaceholder("history"), ("human", "{question}"), ]) def build_context(state, retriever, store, llm): docs = retriever.invoke(state["question"]) mems = store.search(("users", state["user_id"]), query=state["question"], limit=3) history = trim_messages(state["messages"], max_tokens=4000, strategy="last", token_counter=llm, start_on="human") return prompt.invoke({ "product": "Acme Cloud", "docs": "\n\n".join(d.page_content for d in docs), "memory": "\n".join(m.value["text"] for m in mems), "history": history, "question": state["question"], }) PROMPT Template Role, grounding rule and XML-delimited slots for each context layer. SELECT Retrieve Top documents for the question plus three relevant long-term memories. COMPRESS Trim Keep the most recent history that fits a 4,000-token budget. ASSEMBLE Fill Context fills the template's slots; the result goes to the model.

Slide 16: Evaluating Prompts vs Context

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Evaluating Prompts vs Context Measure each layer separately so you know what to fix Prompt evaluation • Golden test set of inputs with expected outputs • Instruction and format adherence rate • A/B compare prompt variants on the same set • Regression-test every prompt change Context evaluation • Retrieval precision and recall: were the right chunks found? • Faithfulness: is the answer grounded in the context? • Tokens and cost per turn against the budget • Task success across long, multi-turn runs Debug in this order: if the right information was not in the window, fix the context first. If it was there and the answer is still wrong, fix the prompt.

Slide 17: Key Takeaways

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Key Takeaways Prompt engineering crafts the sentence. Context engineering builds the system. 1 Prompt engineering is a subset of context engineering, not its rival. 2 Prompting alone suits clear, self-contained tasks; add context engineering for knowledge, memory, tools and many turns. 3 Treat the window as a finite budget: the smallest set of high-signal tokens wins. 4 Write, select, compress, isolate — and design against poisoning, distraction, confusion and clash. 5 Evaluate retrieval and instructions separately so you know which layer to fix.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between prompt engineering and context engineering?

Prompt engineering designs the instructions, examples, constraints, and output format. Context engineering manages the broader information supplied to the model, including retrieved knowledge, memory, tools, and conversation history.

Does context engineering replace prompt engineering?

No. The deck presents prompt engineering as a layer within context engineering. A well-assembled context still needs clear instructions about the task and the required answer.

What are the four context engineering strategies?

Write saves useful information outside the active window. Select retrieves what the current step needs. Compress trims or summarizes information. Isolate separates subtasks or state into different contexts.

When is prompt engineering alone sufficient?

Self-contained tasks that mainly need clear instructions, tone, or output formatting can often begin with prompt design. Tasks needing external knowledge, persistent memory, tools, or multiple turns also require context management.

Why can longer context create problems?

A larger window may contain irrelevant, stale, contradictory, or erroneous material. The deck discusses missed information, distraction, confusion, poisoning, and context clash as reasons to curate what enters each turn.

How should prompt and context quality be evaluated?

Evaluate instruction and format adherence separately from retrieval quality, grounding, token use, and multi-turn task success. If necessary information is missing, fix retrieval or context assembly first; if it is present, investigate the instructions and output behavior.
